title: Norway Seeks Temporary Ban on Smart Glasses
paragraphs: Smart glasses can snap photos, record conversations or stream video online — all without the people in range of their cameras and microphones knowing anything.
These privacy concerns have prompted Norway's government to consider asking its parliament, the Storting, to put a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places.
Norwegian authorities say a ban could apply to places where "privacy is particularly important," like healthcare facilities, or fitness centers with changing rooms and showers.

Places where children gather, such as schools, kindergartens and playgrounds, are also a major focus. The restrictions could also extend to public concerts and sports events, parks, beaches, museums and shopping centers.

​​The government said it's not proposing a complete ban, however. Smart glasses would still be allowed in some places and for private use, while exceptions are being considered for people with disabilities.
A temporary ban would give authorities time to decide what devices might be affected, and whether permanent regulation is needed.
The government says it plans to put the proposal before parliament "as soon as possible."

Adam Smith of British advocacy group Privacy International said the move is "a welcome protection against big tech's greedy attempts to extract ever more data, often in absence of any thought for the privacy or rights of others."
He added that people don't expect to be secretly recorded while going about their daily lives.
Meta, which produces AI glasses with eyewear company Ray-Ban, tells users to respect other people's privacy and stop recording if someone objects.
The company says a light on the glasses shows when recording is happening, and if the glasses detect that the light has been blocked or tampered with, the camera is automatically disabled.
However, such assurances haven't satisfied everybody.
In fact, Dutch eyewear company Hans Anders has suspended sales of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses because it's concerned about the debate around them.
And in Britain, the UK Cinema Association said in August it was introducing policies to prohibit or restrict camera-enabled smart glasses, because of concerns about privacy and film piracy.
